clue.text: Have a drink; it will lessen the shock

definitions.meaning: a brimming glass of drink, filled to the top for a toast
a fender on a car or a buffer that absorbs an impact

explanation.surface: A stiff drink as a remedy for a nasty shock.
explanation.definitionFit: A full glass raised in a toast and a car's impact-absorbing bar share this name.

clue.text: South American whose heart was wooed by Viola

definitions.text: South American whose heart was wooed by Viola

parts.words: South American whose heart was wooed by Viola
parts.note: in Twelfth Night, Viola disguised as a page woos the countess Olivia on Orsino's behalf, and that name sits in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: A Latin American's heart won by a woman called Viola.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'heart' is literal: the countess Olivia, whom Viola woos in Twelfth Night, sits in the middle of the word, between B and N.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Andean republic named after Simón Bolívar is South American.

clue.text: The chap with Kitty has a lace shawl

parts.note: a kitty is a pool of cash, as kept in a till

explanation.surface: A man and a woman named Kitty share a lace shawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' looks like a girl's name; it is a cash fund, the till.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish lace scarf worn over the head and shoulders.

clue.text: Axe Bunter when he so full of spirit ?

indicators.note: asks for Bunter in an excited, jumbled state, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: Billy Bunter getting the sack while in high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When he so' tells us to jumble AXE BUNTER. Billy Bunter is the greedy fat schoolboy of Frank Richards' Greyfriars stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bubbling with high spirits and lively energy.

clue.text: Bowlers are tops

definitions.meaning: in cricket, slow bowlers who turn the ball off the pitch
toys that twirl on their points

explanation.surface: A claim that bowlers are the best players.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket's slow turning bowlers and twirling toys share the name.

clue.text: "Nor you, ye impute to These the fault " (Gray)

definitions.text: "Nor you, ye impute to These the fault " (Gray)

parts.words: Nor you, ye impute to These the fault
parts.note: the missing word in Gray's Elegy addresses the haughty rich

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Gray.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard has 'Nor you, ye Proud, impute to these the fault'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray addresses the haughty and lofty, scorning the humble graves.

clue.text: This organ detects 13

parts.note: 13 across is a scent, so the organ meant is the nose

explanation.surface: An organ that picks up a clue's answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 across is REDOLENCE, a smell, detected by the nose; the answer is the adjective for that organ.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective for the nose describes the organ of smell.

clue.text: Looking for slippery customers in the studios ?

definitions.text: Looking for slippery customers in the studios ?

parts.words: Looking for slippery customers in the studios
parts.note: fishing for slippery eels gives a word sounding like the London film studios

explanation.surface: Searching a film studio for shady characters.
explanation.walkthrough: Ealing Studios are the west London film studios; the name sounds like 'eeling', hunting slippery eels.
explanation.definitionFit: The west London film studios share the sound of catching eels.

clue.text: One set about another perhaps in so many lines …

indicators.note: the letters are moved around and rearranged

explanation.surface: Arranging one set of things against another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' mixes SET and another SET; 'perhaps' warns the order is open.
explanation.definitionFit: Six lines of verse, as in the closing part of a sonnet.

clue.text: Queue for work by platelayers ?

definitions.meaning: railway workers lay track, putting the line in place

explanation.surface: Railway workmen waiting in a queue for their next job.
explanation.definitionFit: A row of waiting people, and the act of laying a railway line into position.

clue.text: It comforts one just to look at the fish !

parts.note: to con is to study or pore over

explanation.surface: Watching fish in a tank is a soothing pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: To comfort someone in grief is to console them.

clue.text: Cover for a prayer-book

definitions.meaning: a book of devotions for lay people

explanation.surface: The binding of a prayer-book.
explanation.definitionFit: A first coat of paint and an old devotional book share the name.

clue.text: Wordsworth's cuckoo was a wandering one

definitions.text: Wordsworth's cuckoo was a wandering one

parts.words: Wordsworth's cuckoo was a wandering one
parts.note: Wordsworth's poem To the Cuckoo asks whether to call the bird a bird or but a wandering sound heard in the air

explanation.surface: A literary note about a poet's cuckoo.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is 'O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird, Or but a wandering Voice?' from Wordsworth's To the Cuckoo.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem calls the unseen bird a wandering sound that speaks, that is, a call heard but not seen.

clue.text: That which causes an inspiring association ?

definitions.text: That which causes an inspiring association

parts.words: That which causes an inspiring association
parts.note: inspiring is read literally as breathing in: a scent that calls up memories as one inhales

explanation.surface: Something that stirs uplifting memories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' looks like 'uplifting' but means inhaling: a smell evokes associations when breathed in.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong scent or suggestiveness that evokes memories when breathed in.

clue.text: What ails one, Craig ?.

explanation.surface: Someone asks a friend named Craig what is wrong with him.
explanation.walkthrough: Craig is not a man: Ailsa Craig is a rocky island in the Firth of Clyde, so the answer is the word before 'Craig'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ailsa Craig is the Scottish island rock, so this is the first part of its name, completing the phrase.

clue.text: Is it for sticking into diagrams of the Terraces ?

definitions.text: Is it for sticking into diagrams of the Terraces ?

parts.words: Is it for sticking into diagrams of the Terraces
parts.note: a pin stuck into charts, and the name of the Terraces at London Zoo

explanation.surface: A question about pinning plans of some terraces.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mappin Terraces are the mock mountain enclosures at London Zoo; split, the name is a pin pushed into charts.
explanation.definitionFit: The zoo's Terraces are named after it, and split it is a pin for a chart.

clue.text: Letters bequeathed we hear ?

indicators.note: says the word is judged by its sound

explanation.surface: Correspondence left in a will.
explanation.walkthrough: The Paston Letters are a famous 15th-century collection of a Norfolk family's correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: The medieval Norfolk family's correspondence is known as their Letters.

clue.text: Acknowledged by the Doctor in the matter of horseflesh

definitions.text: Acknowledged by the Doctor in the matter of horseflesh

parts.words: Acknowledged by the Doctor in the matter of horseflesh
parts.note: Dr Johnson's dictionary defined pastern wrongly; asked why, he admitted his lack of knowledge

explanation.surface: A doctor admitting something about horses.
explanation.walkthrough: The Doctor is Samuel Johnson: asked why his Dictionary defined pastern as a horse's knee, he replied 'Ignorance, madam, pure ignorance.'
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson confessed not knowing a horse's anatomy, admitting lack of knowledge.

clue.text: A lady in a mess ? There's more than one!

indicators.note: the lady sits inside the mess

explanation.surface: A lady caught in a muddle, and she's not alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The French plural for ladies, more than one madame.

clue.text: Takes it all back about those pamphlets

explanation.surface: Someone withdrawing a claim made in some pamphlets.
explanation.definitionFit: Withdrawing a statement is unsaying it, taking it all back.

clue.text: " Was everything by and nothing long " (Dryden)

definitions.text: " Was everything by and nothing long " (Dryden)

parts.words: Was everything by and nothing long
parts.note: the missing word in Dryden's portrait of Zimri, a man who did everything in fits and bursts

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Dryden.
explanation.walkthrough: Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel says of Zimri: 'Was everything by starts, and nothing long'.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation needs a word for fits and bursts, sudden beginnings never followed through.

clue.text: She is related to a Pawnee

definitions.text: She is related to a Pawnee

parts.words: She is related to a Pawnee
parts.note: a pawnee is one who takes goods in pawn, a pawnbroker, and a pawnbroker is nicknamed uncle

explanation.surface: A woman with a Native American relative.
explanation.walkthrough: Pawnee looks like the Native American people; here it is a pawnbroker, called 'uncle' in slang, so she is his brother's or sister's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is the girl related to her uncle.

clue.text: Masculine skills are beaters!

explanation.surface: Manly skills prevail over everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beaters' suggests winners or game beaters; it is organs that beat.
explanation.definitionFit: The organs that pump blood beat, so they are beaters.

clue.text: Macaulay's man at the wheel ?

parts.note: the wheel is the craftsman's turning wheel for shaping clay, not a ship's helm

explanation.surface: A driver or helmsman from Macaulay's writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man at the wheel' suggests a driver or helmsman; it is the craftsman who throws clay on a turning wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of clay pots works at a turning wheel.

clue.text: Whereabouts of the missing boss, according to the office-boy ?

definitions.text: Whereabouts of the missing boss, according to the office-boy ?

parts.words: Whereabouts of the missing boss, according to the office-boy
parts.note: the Latin phrase read as office slang: the boss is out of the office

explanation.surface: An office junior explains where the absent boss has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase means 'by virtue of office', but heard as the office-boy might say it, it means 'away from the office'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase meaning by right of position sounds like 'out of the office'.

clue.text: It's the visage to a T from this aspect

explanation.surface: From this angle the face suits someone to a T.
explanation.definitionFit: One side of a gem or a matter is one aspect.

clue.text: French leave

parts.note: not slipping away unannounced but the French word for leave or dismissal

explanation.surface: Taking off without permission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French leave' is an idiom for leaving without permission; here it is literally the French word for leave.
explanation.definitionFit: The French term for a leave-taking or dismissal, used in English too.

clue.text: Quite a problem for the bicyclist!

definitions.meaning: in geometry, an extra problem following from a proposition

explanation.surface: Something gives a cyclist real trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A follow-on problem in geometry, and one mounted on a bike, share the name.

clue.text: Holding it back inside in these days?

definitions.text: Holding it back inside in these days?

indicators.note: the word for these days holds the other piece within it

parts.note: recent means of these days, lately

indicators.note: the word it is read backwards before going in

explanation.surface: Keeping things bottled up, as people do nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding' puts TI, 'it' turned round by 'back', inside RECENT; the whole clue also describes a person keeping things back.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserved person keeps thoughts held back and unspoken.

clue.text: Coming like a pithy saying from Zurich!

definitions.meaning: aphoristic, in the style of a maxim
the Gnomes of Zurich are Swiss bankers

explanation.surface: Wise words coming out of Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnomes of Zurich' is a nickname for Swiss bankers, so anything from them belongs to the gnomes.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphoristic sayings are terse maxims, and the bankers of Zurich are nicknamed gnomes.

clue.text: They are bound to make secure knots

explanation.surface: Sailors tying knots that hold fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Guarantors are bound by a legal pledge to pay if another defaults.

clue.text: Carroll's knowing little boy gets a nap!

definitions.meaning: the Duchess's song in Alice: the boy sneezes because he knows it annoys
cloth is combed to raise a nap

explanation.surface: A child from Lewis Carroll is put down for a rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duchess sings 'He only does it to annoy, Because he knows it teases'. 'Nap' is not sleep but the raised fibres on cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's boy knows his sneezing annoys, and cloth is combed up to raise its pile.
